strengths: Extremely thorough and careful experimental methodology: the paper goes well beyond typical practice by tuning AlphaZero's rollout count for fairness (Appendix G), verifying the reliability of the Pgx baseline implementation against an independent open-source AlphaZero (Appendix F), reporting wall-clock inference time parity (Appendix H), and providing head-to-head matches against classic engines GnuGo and Pachi (Appendix I). This level of rigor substantially strengthens the credibility of the efficiency claims.

The core algorithmic idea—directly modeling the action-value function with a neural network (bridging the gap left by removing tree-search based Q backups) combined with reverse KL and entropy regularization and λ-returns—is clean, well-motivated, and has an elegant closed-form solution (Theorem A.2), making implementation straightforward.

Comprehensive ablation study (Figure 6/Table 2) convincingly isolates the contribution of each of the three components (KL regularization, entropy regularization, λ-returns), with clear qualitative explanations (e.g., entropy collapse in 'KL Only' variant, Figure 7).

Evaluation spans five diverse board games plus a large-scale 19x19 Go experiment, and additional analyses (sensitivity to hyperparameters, bias-variance tradeoff validation, convergence to quantal response equilibrium in a toy game) add depth and support the theoretical motivations empirically.

Honest and clearly stated limitations: the authors explicitly note that their claims are about learning efficiency/sample efficiency, not necessarily asymptotic superiority over search-based methods with unlimited compute, and back this up with their own experiment (Appendix G.3) showing AlphaZero can match KLENT's performance given ~4-5x more training budget.
weaknesses: The core originality is modest: KL-regularized policy optimization, entropy regularization, and λ-returns are all well-established techniques (MPO, SAC, TD(λ), and the regularized-policy-optimization view of AlphaZero from Grill et al. 2020); the paper itself acknowledges the contribution is primarily empirical rather than a new method. This is a reasonable contribution but somewhat incremental for a top-tier ML venue.

The headline efficiency claims weaken considerably at scale: in the 19x19 Go experiment (Figure 8), KLENT is only described as achieving 'competitive' (not clearly superior) performance versus AlphaZero, in contrast to the strong several-fold gains reported for the medium-scale games — raising questions about whether the method's advantages persist as action/board size grows.

Directly modeling the action-value function Qθ(s,a) as a vector output requires the action space to be small and fixed-size, which may limit applicability to games/domains with very large or variable/combinatorial action spaces (e.g., full 19x19 Go has 361+ actions vs. the 82 tested for 9x9 Go), and this scalability limitation is not deeply analyzed despite the network output growing with |A|.

Evaluation relies substantially on win rate against a single fixed anchored opponent (the Pgx baseline) as a fitness proxy; although the authors supplement this with Elo (with appropriate caveats) and matches against GnuGo/Pachi, the primary learning curves in Figure 5/6 still hinge on one reference opponent per game, which can compress or distort apparent performance differences near ceiling/floor win rates.

Only three random seeds are used per configuration, which is relatively few given the well-known high variance of self-play RL training, and some confidence bands in the main figures appear to overlap substantially between methods (e.g., AlphaZero vs. Gumbel AlphaZero in some games), suggesting some comparisons may not be highly statistically robust.

The paper does not compare against other lookahead-reduced or model-based-but-cheaper baselines beyond Gumbel AlphaZero/TRPO AlphaZero (e.g., MuZero-style or Muesli, which is cited but not benchmarked), leaving open whether KLENT's advantage holds against a wider range of modern efficient search-based competitors.

strengths: Extremely thorough empirical evaluation: five board games plus a 19x19 Go scalability study, three seeds per condition, and a very extensive appendix (hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, bias-variance validation of λ-returns, reliability checks of the Pgx AlphaZero baseline against an independent third-party implementation, rollout-count tuning for AlphaZero, head-to-head matches against GnuGo/Pachi, Elo analysis with appropriate caveats, and convergence analysis to the quantal response equilibrium on a toy game). This level of diligence is commendable and substantially aids reproducibility.

The core policy-update rule (closed-form solution to the KL+entropy regularized optimization problem) is cleanly derived and clearly presented, and the paper is well organized with clear connections to related work (Grill et al., Sokota et al., SAC, MPO, TRPO).

The ablation study convincingly isolates the contribution of each of the three components (KL regularization, entropy regularization, λ-returns), with a clear qualitative explanation of failure modes (entropy collapse in 'KL Only', instability in 'ENT Only').
Honest and appropriately scoped limitations section acknowledging that the method is about efficiency, not necessarily asymptotic superiority over search-based methods with unlimited compute.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the paper itself states 'the novelty of this study lies in our empirical result,' as KL regularization, entropy regularization, and λ-returns are all well-established techniques (MPO, SAC, TD(λ)); the closed-form solution combining reverse-KL and entropy regularization is also already known in the literature (e.g., Vieillard et al. 2020, Sokota et al. 2022). This makes the contribution largely an engineering/empirical combination rather than a conceptual advance.

The flagship large-scale result (19x19 Go, Section 5.3/Figure 8) only shows KLENT reaching performance 'competitive' with (i.e., roughly equal to) AlphaZero, not superior. This is a significant weakening of the central efficiency claim precisely in the regime (large-scale games) where computational savings would matter most and where search-based methods are reported to require the most resources; the paper's headline claims (e.g., Figure 1's fourfold efficiency gain) are not demonstrated at this larger scale.

In the main comparison (Section 5.1, Figure 5), the AlphaZero-family baselines use a fixed MCTS budget of 32 simulations during training across all five games, which was not swept/tuned per game; the authors' own Appendix G analysis (conducted only for 9x9/19x19 Go) shows that 8–16 rollouts are actually more efficient than 32 for AlphaZero, suggesting the main baseline comparisons for Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, Hex, and Othello may be based on a suboptimal (and therefore less competitive) configuration for the search-based baselines, potentially inflating KLENT's apparent advantage.

The approach requires explicitly modeling an action-value head that outputs a value for every action in a finite action space and explicitly summing over all actions to compute the softmax policy and value bootstrap (Eq. 3, 6); this limits applicability to settings with very large or unbounded/combinatorial action spaces (e.g., many real-world domains the introduction motivates, such as matrix multiplication discovery or algorithm design, which can have enormous action spaces), somewhat undercutting the broader applicability claims made in the introduction.

DQN and PPO, the model-free baselines, are comparatively weak/under-tuned implementations (hyperparameters taken largely as-is from Stable-Baselines3 defaults) and are not core competitors to the paper's actual target (search-based methods); their weak performance contributes to the 'Average Performance Across Environments' headline plot in a way that may be somewhat misleading about the true margin of improvement over the strongest baselines (Gumbel AlphaZero).

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across five diverse board games (Animal Shogi, Gardner Chess, 9x9 Go, Hex, Othello) plus a large-scale 19x19 Go experiment, with multiple random seeds and clear efficiency gains over AlphaZero-family and model-free baselines (DQN, PPO).

Extensive and thoughtful ablation study that isolates the contribution of each of the three core components (KL regularization, entropy regularization, λ-returns), with interpretable diagnostics such as policy entropy collapse in the 'KL Only' variant.

Strong effort toward fair and credible baselines: the authors verify the reliability of their AlphaZero (Pgx) implementation against an independent open-source implementation, and perform extensive rollout-count/training-budget sweeps for AlphaZero so that the comparison is not against an under-tuned baseline.

Solid theoretical grounding: closed-form derivation of the optimal regularized policy (with full proof in the appendix) and an empirical/theoretical connection to quantal response equilibria, validated on a small analytically tractable game.

Thorough appendix addressing reproducibility and robustness concerns: hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, wall-clock timing comparisons, Elo analysis with appropriate caveats about its limitations, head-to-head matches against classic engines (GnuGo, Pachi), and test-time search scaling experiments.

Clear writing and figures, with a well-motivated research question (can model-free RL match search-based RL efficiency in board games) that is practically significant given the computational cost barriers of AlphaZero-style training.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a combination of existing techniques (reverse KL regularization, entropy regularization, λ-returns) rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the authors themselves state the novelty lies primarily in the empirical demonstration, which somewhat limits the originality claim.

Directly modeling the Q-function over the full action space requires enumerating all actions for both the softmax policy computation and the value bootstrap; it is unclear how this approach would scale to domains with very large or combinatorial action spaces (e.g., full 19x19 Go has a much larger action space than the games tested, and the paper's claimed extension to domains like discrete optimization or theorem proving is not empirically tested).

The model-free baselines (DQN, PPO) appear to use largely default/Stable-Baselines3-derived hyperparameters without the same level of extensive tuning effort given to the AlphaZero-family baselines (which received dedicated rollout-count and budget sweeps), raising a potential fairness asymmetry in the comparison.

The claim of 'completely eliminating' search during training is somewhat tempered by Appendix H, which shows that adding test-time MCTS further improves KLENT-trained networks, suggesting search remains valuable even if not required during training — this nuance could be stated more prominently in the main text.

Hyperparameters (α, β, λ) were unified across games, but the sensitivity analysis in Appendix D is only conducted in 9x9 Go, leaving open whether this robustness generalizes to the other four environments or to substantially different game structures.

Evaluation relies primarily on fixed anchored opponents (Pgx baseline checkpoints) rather than round-robin tournaments among all trained agents or against a diverse pool of opponents, which could leave open questions about generalization of learned policies beyond the specific evaluation opponent.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical analysis of the combination of reverse-KL and entropy regularization in two settings: local linear convergence in normal-form zero-sum games (with a tighter condition than prior work by Sokota et al. 2022, clearly illustrated in Figure 3) and convergence to the entropy-regularized (quantal response) equilibrium in finite-length sequential games via backward induction. Both results are supported by careful proofs in the appendix and verified with clean numerical experiments (Matching Pennies, Count-Up Game) that match theory closely.

The empirical evaluation is extensive and well-executed: five board games of varying branching factor, multiple strong search-based (AlphaZero, TRPO AlphaZero, Gumbel AlphaZero) and model-free (DQN, PPO) baselines, consistent architectures/compute budgets, 3 seeds, and a large appendix with many robustness checks (hyperparameter sensitivity, network architecture ablations, comparisons to Discrete SAC/V-MPO/Munchausen DQN/GRPO, implementation reliability checks against alpha-zero-general and Pachi/GnuGo, Elo analysis, scaling with test-time MCTS, and a 19x19 Go large-scale experiment).

The core algorithmic idea is simple, well-motivated, and clearly explained, with a fully derived closed-form policy update (Theorem A.2) that eliminates the need for MCTS during training, and the ablation study (Fig. 7-9) convincingly isolates the contribution of each of the three components (reverse-KL, entropy, λ-returns).

The paper is transparent about its contribution scope (revisiting/characterizing rather than proposing new algorithmic ingredients) and includes an honest limitations discussion noting that efficiency gains do not necessarily imply superior asymptotic performance with unlimited compute, which is further substantiated by the AlphaZero training-budget scaling experiment in Appendix L.3 showing AlphaZero eventually catches up given ~4-5x more compute.
weaknesses: Theorem 5.1's convergence guarantee for normal-form games is a sufficient (not necessary) local condition, and it is unclear how this local analysis connects rigorously to the practical algorithm's global behavior in high-dimensional sequential games with function approximation; the finite-length game theorem (Theorem C.12) is a tabular/exact backward-induction result that does not account for neural network approximation error, non-stationarity from concurrent Q-learning, or the λ-return estimator, so the gap between theory and the practical deep RL algorithm (Algorithm 1) is not formally bridged.

The main efficiency claims rest heavily on a single implementation of AlphaZero-family baselines (Pgx/Mctx), and although Appendix K/L provide useful sanity checks, the substantial performance gap versus search-based methods (especially in Go/Hex) could partly reflect baseline hyperparameter choices (e.g., fixed 32 simulations per move during training) rather than a fundamental limitation of search-based methods; the appendix's own rollout-count sweep (L.1) shows AlphaZero's efficiency is highly sensitive to this choice, raising the question of whether the main comparison used an optimally tuned baseline.

Novelty is incremental: the regularized objective (reverse-KL + entropy) and its closed-form solution are already known from MPO/V-MPO and Vieillard et al./Sokota et al./Zhan et al., and the practical algorithm largely substitutes MCTS-derived targets in AlphaZero-style pipelines with an analytical softmax update plus λ-return value learning — a natural but relatively straightforward combination of existing ideas, as the authors themselves acknowledge.

The experiments are restricted to the family of two-player, perfect-information, finite deterministic board games; despite the discussion of extensions to stochastic environments and continuous actions in the appendix, no empirical evidence is given for these settings, leaving the generality claim in the introduction (applicability to discrete optimization, algorithmic discovery, math proving) largely speculative.

Some presentation issues: Figure 3's caption/subfigure labeling is a bit confusing (duplicate panel labels across the LaTeX source), and the extensive appendix (31 pages) suggests the core paper's self-contained evidentiary value is limited without heavy reliance on supplementary material that reviewers/readers must cross-reference to fully evaluate robustness claims.

strengths: Provides a rigorous theoretical treatment of reverse-KL + entropy regularized policy optimization in two-player settings, including a tightened local linear convergence condition for normal-form games (strictly generalizing the bound in Sokota et al. 2022) and a backward-induction convergence proof for finite-length games, both backed by clean proofs in the appendix.

Theoretical claims are empirically verified with well-designed synthetic experiments (Matching Pennies, Count-Up Game) that visually and numerically match the predicted convergence boundaries and quantal-response-equilibrium limits.

The resulting practical algorithm (KLENT) is evaluated extensively on five board games plus 19x19 Go, showing consistent and substantial (up to 4x) training-efficiency gains over AlphaZero-family baselines without requiring search during training, with reasonable control for simulator-evaluation budgets.

The appendix contains an unusually thorough set of robustness checks: ablations isolating KL regularization, entropy regularization, and λ-returns; sensitivity analysis over (α,β,λ); architecture ablations; comparisons against additional baselines (Discrete SAC, V-MPO, Munchausen DQN, GRPO, forward-KL variant); verification of baseline implementation reliability against an independent AlphaZero implementation; rollout-count and training-budget scaling studies for AlphaZero showing the efficiency gap persists even when AlphaZero is tuned/given much larger budgets; and head-to-head matches against GnuGo/Pachi.

The paper is transparent about the scope of its contribution (explicitly stating it does not introduce new algorithmic ingredients) and honestly discusses the limitation that efficiency gains do not necessarily imply superior asymptotic performance.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic idea (combining reverse-KL and entropy regularization) is not new and has been analyzed before by Vieillard et al. (2020a), Sokota et al. (2022), and Zhan et al. (2023); the paper's main theoretical novelty is a quantitatively broader convergence region and an application to two-player games, which, while useful, is an incremental rather than conceptual advance.

There is a non-trivial gap between the idealized theoretical settings (exact Q-values, exact normal-form/finite-length game updates, no function approximation or sampling error) and the practical deep-RL instantiation (KLENT uses learned, approximate Q and policy networks with λ-returns and minibatch SGD); no convergence guarantee is given for the practical algorithm itself, so the theory serves mainly as motivating intuition rather than a guarantee for the method actually deployed.

The efficiency comparison is based on simulator-evaluation counts; although the appendix adds wall-clock timing and AlphaZero rollout/budget sweeps that support the central efficiency claim, the framing in the main text ('achieves stable and competitive learning with significantly fewer training resources') could be read as a stronger general claim than what is empirically shown (i.e., AlphaZero eventually reaches comparable performance given 4-5x more compute in 9x9 Go, per Appendix L).

Evaluation relies heavily on a single anchored-opponent win-rate metric using one specific set of pretrained Pgx baselines; despite supplementary Elo and head-to-head matches against GnuGo/Pachi, broader validation (e.g., against stronger/more diverse opponents, or human-level benchmarks) is limited, and Elo-based comparisons are explicitly flagged by the authors as unreliable across different tournament pools.

The practical novelty of KLENT itself is modest—an actor-critic-style method with an analytic regularized policy target and λ-return value learning—closely related to existing methods (MPO, V-MPO, SAC variants); its main distinguishing feature is the specific combination and application to self-play board games rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

strengths: The paper provides a coherent combination of theoretical and empirical analysis of a specific, well-motivated regularization scheme (reverse-KL + entropy), rather than only empirical tuning or only abstract theory.

Theorem 5.1 provides a strictly broader convergence guarantee region than the prior result of Sokota et al. (2022) for normal-form games, with a clean and well-documented proof (Appendix C.1) based on a weighted-norm Jacobian contraction argument, including an extension to general-sum games (Theorem C.10).
The finite-length game convergence result (Theorem C.12) via backward induction is intuitive and matches the empirical Count-Up Game experiment closely, lending credibility to the theoretical claims.

The empirical evaluation is unusually comprehensive for a methods paper: five board games of varying branching factor, a large-scale 19x19 Go experiment, extensive ablations isolating the roles of KL regularization, entropy regularization, and λ-returns, and dozens of additional appendix experiments (hyperparameter sensitivity, network architecture ablations, comparisons to Discrete SAC/V-MPO/Munchausen DQN/GRPO, alternative AlphaZero implementations, rollout-count tuning, extended training budgets, test-time MCTS scaling, head-to-head matches against Pachi/GnuGo, Elo analysis with appropriate caveats).

The authors are careful and transparent about limitations: they explicitly note their contribution is a new theoretical/empirical characterization rather than a new algorithmic ingredient, they show AlphaZero eventually catches up in win rate with enough training budget (Appendix L.3), and they discuss generalizability conditions (stochastic environments, continuous actions) without overclaiming.

The efficiency gains (up to 4x fewer simulator evaluations to reach comparable performance, and consistent advantages in high-branching-factor games like Go and Hex) are practically meaningful and could be useful for resource-constrained practitioners.
weaknesses: The core theoretical results establish only local linear convergence around a fixed point; since actual self-play training starts far from the equilibrium, it is unclear how informative this local guarantee is for the global training trajectories observed in the deep RL experiments.

There is a significant gap between the clean theoretical setting (exact Q-functions, tabular/normal-form games) and the practical algorithm (neural network function approximation, λ-return estimates, finite replay buffers); the paper does not formally characterize how approximation and estimation error affect the proven convergence guarantees.

The central algorithmic ingredients (reverse-KL regularization, entropy regularization, λ-returns) are all individually well established in prior literature (MPO, SAC, TD(λ)), and the authors themselves state the contribution is a new characterization rather than new ingredients; this reduces the originality of the empirical contribution to an engineering combination, even though the combination is shown to be effective.

Despite the "pure model-free" framing, Table 2 shows that KLENT still benefits substantially from test-time MCTS (e.g., 9x9 Go win rate jumps from an implicit lower baseline to 89% with search), which somewhat tempers the narrative that search can be fully eliminated, though this nuance is disclosed.

On the largest-scale environment (19x19 Go), KLENT achieves only "competitive" (roughly on-par) performance with AlphaZero rather than a clear efficiency advantage, raising some question about how the efficiency gains scale to very large action/state spaces.

Reliance on a third-party reimplementation (Pgx/Mctx) for AlphaZero-family baselines, rather than the original AlphaZero/Gumbel AlphaZero codebases, introduces some residual reproducibility risk, although the authors provide substantial supporting validation in the appendix.
